Mengxiao Wang, Mahbub Alam, Kalyan Nakka, and Nitesh Saxena Affiliation: Texas A&M University Affiliation: {jacksonwang, mahbub.alam, kalyan, nsaxena}@tamu.edu
Abstract

Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit’s coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify.

In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. As part of the framework, Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based agents collect reports and build replications, an agent from another vendor reviews each build, and code decides whether harm occurred. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications.11 1 A list of all incidents that we studied, with their sources and replications, can be accessed at https://rogue-ai.surge.sh. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents now run shell commands, change cloud servers and pay out cryptocurrency for their users. Anthropic’s coding agent Claude Code [1] ran terraform destroy and removed the production stack of DataTalks.Club [2]. In September 2026, the Australian government opened an investigation after an OpenAI agent accessed government health portals, including Medicare statistics [3]. News stories and company posts report such failures, but a report describes the outcome and rarely the mechanism. The deletion could come from a careless model, too much authority or a misunderstood task, each with its own fix. Security researchers already re-run attacks that made the news [4], and agent incidents can be tested the same way. A replication cannot see the company’s logs, but it can test whether the harm occurs with the cause that the report names and stops once that cause is removed.

Prior work collects, labels or reruns these incidents but does not test their causes. Incident catalogs such as the AI Incident Database and the Agent Incident Registry collect and label reports without testing them [5, 6, 7], and agent benchmarks build their test cases from attacks or tasks that their authors design [8, 9]. Closer to replication, Chronicle reruns parts of six recorded failures with simulated model outputs [10], Squidbrake reruns the commands of 12 incidents against its rules [11], and CVE-Genie reproduces software exploits, whose result does not depend on a model’s choice [12]. However, an agent incident depends on a model’s decision, which can change from run to run. A single rebuild therefore cannot show that the cause named in a report produced the harm, and none of these methods compares the rebuild with a control that lacks only that cause.

For example, in July 2025, Replit’s coding agent deleted the production database of SaaStr during a code freeze [13, 14], and the report blames a database that the agent’s development work shared with the live site. As Figure 1 shows, we rebuild the incident offline as a repository whose tests use the production database, together with a matched control whose tests use a temporary database. The two copies differ only in the blamed cause, so a difference in harm between them is evidence for that cause. Current models wiped the production rows in about half of the incident sessions, while all 15 control sessions kept their rows, which supports the report’s claim. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI, the first framework that tests public reports of agent incidents by controlled replication. Unlike CVE-Genie and Chronicle, ROGUE-AI compares each rebuild with a matched control and runs current models repeatedly in each condition.

ROGUE-AI is a pipeline of LLM agents with one job each, which we call specialist agents. Agents search the web for reports, check each report against its most detailed source and write down the named cause. Other agents build the replication and its control, an agent from another vendor reviews each build, and code decides whether harm occurred. From 253 reports, Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based agents built 108 replications of 96 incidents in 38 classes, at $3.28 each. ROGUE-AI reproduced the reported harm in 89% of its replications (§6.2), and five models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and DeepSeek still made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of incident sessions, against at most 1% in the controls (Table 4). In the replication of the Medicare incident, for example, the five models entered the portal’s restricted area with the browser’s saved sign-in in 14 of 15 incident sessions and in none of the 30 control sessions. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no attacker, and in these 62, an agent that did what its task asked missed an ordinary hazard, such as the shared database (§5).

Defenses against prompt injection miss most of this harm. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models, but they contain no injected instruction, which is what these defenses look for. Defenses taken from the reports did better, and with confirmation by the user or data-flow tracking, the five models caused no harm. Checks that match the text of an action were weaker, because rephrased attacks still caused part of the harm (§6.4). Because a replication finds the hazard, it also suggests a fix. We added a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence, such as a warning that the tests drop the production database. This warning lowered harm for all five models, to 2% for Claude Sonnet 4.6, whereas most harm remained with a restated rule, with a note that gives only the fact, or with a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard (§6.3). Agent builders should keep production credentials out of the agent’s reach, and vendors can rerun the replications before each release. We make four contributions:

  • •

    Controlled Replication of Security Incidents Reported in Media. We introduce ROGUE-AI, the first framework that tests a reported agent incident by rebuilding it offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause. Agents repeated the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% in the controls (§3, §6).

  • •

    Multi-Agent Replication Pipeline. We build the pipeline from Claude-, Gemini- and GPT-based specialist agents, which find and verify reports, build each replication, and diagnose and fix failed replications. Because these agents can fail like those they test, each judgment has an independent check, and code decides harm. They built 108 replications from 253 reports, and vendors can rerun them to audit a new model for $0.54 to $47 (§4, §6). We release ROGUE-AI’s code, replications and session logs [15], and we reported each model’s results to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and DeepSeek.

  • •

    Ordinary Causes of Reported Harm. We show that current models repeat reported harm for ordinary reasons, such as a hazard that the agent never saw. One edit at the first harmful step removed the harm in 118 of 208 harmful sessions, and replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models (§6, §6.3, §6.4).

  • •

    Hazard Warnings as a Mitigation. We propose a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence. The warning lowered harm for all five models, to 2% for Claude Sonnet 4.6, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left harm between 83% and 98% (§6.3).

2 Background and Criteria

LLM Agents and Their Incidents. By an LLM agent we mean a program in which a language model decides which tools to call and acts on the results [16]. A coding agent runs shell commands, a personal assistant sends and deletes mail, a browser agent fills in web forms, and a wallet agent signs transfers. Many agents also load tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which lets them call tools published by other parties. We count an event as an agent incident if an LLM agent took an action through a tool and that action caused harm or achieved an attacker’s goal against a victim, and if the event was first reported between January 2025 and October 2026. Harm in the wild, demonstrations on shipped products, threat reports and vendor evaluations qualify, but events on research prototypes do not.

Running Example. We follow the Replit incident throughout [13]. The user had told the agent many times to make no change without permission [14]. During this code freeze, the agent’s commands deleted the production database, and Replit’s CEO confirmed the deletion. Nobody attacked the agent, which had a standing rule against changes, a task that seemed to need a database change, and production credentials.

Criteria for a Replication. To test such a report, a replication has to meet six criteria, which follow from how reports and agents fail. First, the report is checked against a primary source, since we had to correct 76 of 253 incident records and found 2 contradicted by their sources. Second, a current model makes the incident’s decision again, because rerunning the recorded commands tests only the commands. Third, a matched control removes only the hazard, because the task alone can produce harm that should not count toward the reported cause. Fourth, code decides harm from the environment’s state, because agents misreport their actions, as the Replit agent did [14]. Fifth, a pipeline builds the test from the report, because new reports arrive weekly. Sixth, the test runs offline on any model, letting a vendor rerun it before a release.

Comparison with Prior Work. As Table 1 shows, no prior work meets the criteria that we can check from its publications. Benchmarks run current models, and AgentDojo runs its tasks with and without the injection. Their test cases, however, come from the benchmarks’ authors. Chronicle needs a recorded run and simulates the model’s outputs, and Squidbrake reruns reported commands against its rules.

Closest in method is CVE-Genie [12], which reproduced 428 of 841 CVEs at an average cost of $2.77. Developer agents set up the software and write an exploit, critic agents review the steps, and a verifier checks a signal specific to the vulnerability. The target of CVE-Genie, however, is software, where the result of an exploit does not depend on a model’s choice. In an agent incident, by contrast, the test concerns a model’s decision, which varies between models and runs, and the task alone can cause harm. ROGUE-AI therefore adds a matched control, repeated runs on any model and a statistical test for each claim (§3).

3 The ROGUE-AI Framework

Reports as Claims. In ROGUE-AI, we treat an incident report as a causal claim and a replication as a controlled experiment that tests the claim. We write the claim of a report RR as C⁡(R)=⟨T,E,H,a∗,h⟩C(R)=\langle T,E,H,a^{*},h\rangle. The claim states that in an environment EE that contains a hazard HH, an agent given the task TT takes the action a∗a^{*}, which causes the harm hh. For the Replit report, TT is fixing a bug in a demo application, EE is a repository under a code freeze, HH is a test suite that shares the production database, a∗a^{*} is running the tests, and hh is the loss of production rows. The hazard is the part of the environment that the report blames. The claim is causal, as the report asserts that an agent causes hh more often with HH present than with HH absent. For a model MM, we write this difference as

τM=Pr⁡[h∣do⁡(H)]−Pr⁡[h∣do⁡(¬H)],\tau_{M}=\Pr[h\mid\mathrm{do}(H)]-\Pr[h\mid\mathrm{do}(\neg H)],

where do⁡(⋅)\mathrm{do}(\cdot) marks that the experimenter sets the hazard instead of observing it. A report is correct for MM if τM>0\tau_{M}>0.

Replications as Interventions. In ROGUE-AI, a replication consists of the task TT, a state check and two offline environments EHE_{H} and E¬HE_{\neg H} built from the same world. After a session, the state check inspects the environment and decides whether hh occurred. EHE_{H} is the incident condition, and E¬HE_{\neg H} is the matched control, which keeps the cue (the part that makes a∗a^{*} attractive) and removes only the hazard. In the Replit replication, the control’s tests create their tables in a temporary database. The harm rate of a condition is the share of its sessions with harm. If we run MM for nn sessions in both conditions, the difference between the two harm rates estimates τM\tau_{M}, up to sampling noise.

Validity Conditions. As Table 2 lists, a replication tests the claim only if it meets five conditions. Suppose the hazard is reachable, the harm requires the hazard and the two conditions differ only in the hazard. Then the difference between the harm rates in EHE_{H} and E¬HE_{\neg H} is an unbiased estimate of the hazard’s effect on harm for MM in this replication. Reachability rules out a replication where no model could fail, and the minimal difference rules out a second cause such as a new prompt.

Fidelity to the Report. The other two conditions, a natural path to the hazard and fidelity to the report, do not affect this estimate. They decide whether the replication’s hazard is the report’s hazard, and a replication that fails them tests a different claim. A replication therefore takes only the elements that the report and its primary sources state. The replication fills omitted details, such as the model or system prompt, with marked neutral defaults and adds no rule, prohibition, pressure or hint, since any of these could change the decision under test. Code checks the first three conditions, a reviewer model checks the natural path, and both check fidelity to the claim card, which ties each element of the claim to a sentence of the report.

Outcomes. For a replication, let ktk_{t} of ntn_{t} incident sessions and kck_{c} of ncn_{c} control sessions cause harm. We compare the two rates with a one-sided Fisher’s exact test and correct all pp-values with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. A replication is supported if the corrected value is below 0.05, suggestive if the incident condition caused harm without reaching this level, and not reproduced if no incident session caused harm. A supported replication thus shows that the cause that the report blames produces the reported harm in agents built on the tested models. Even a replication that is not reproduced bounds the harm rate of its build. With kt=0k_{t}=0, the 95% Wilson upper bound on the harm rate is about 20% for 15 sessions and 11% for 30. We mark a replication as no control if it caused harm but has no finished control session. We can pool the counts over models or stratify the test by model.

Audits. To audit a new model M′M^{\prime}, ROGUE-AI reruns all replications that passed the checks and recomputes the outcomes for M′M^{\prime}. A replication not reproduced for earlier models but supported for M′M^{\prime} is a regression, and the reverse is an improvement. A vendor needs only an adapter for the model’s API to run this audit, because the replications run offline and code decides harm. The audit record puts the harmful sessions of the new model in both conditions next to the results of earlier models, and a vendor can thus see which reported mistakes a release still makes (§6).

4 The ROGUE-AI Pipeline

This section follows a report through ROGUE-AI to an outcome, with the Replit report as the example. ROGUE-AI uses LLM agents as automation tools, and Figure 1 shows where they work. In the first two stages, searcher agents find reports, a screener applies our inclusion rules, a verifier compares each report with a primary source, two labelers label the incident and a report analyst writes down its claim (§4.1). In the third stage, a domain builder writes the replication, and a path reviewer and a domain reviewer check the build (§4.2).

In the last two stages, code runs the validity checks and the models under test run the replication. Code then decides harm and computes the test, and diagnoser agents read the transcripts of replications that fail. The stages are linked by a repair loop, in which reviewers send faulty builds back to the builder, by a diagnose-fix-rerun loop that fixes failed replications (§6.2), and by an audit that reruns the replications on each new model.

We follow three rules so that a mistake of one agent does not reach the results. First, no agent checks its own work. Two labelers from different vendors label each incident, and a model from a vendor other than the builder’s reviews the build. Second, code decides harm from the environment’s final state. Third, each of the seven judgments that agents make has an independent check (Table 3). A person decides in three cases: no agent can confirm a source, three labelers give three values, or a build still fails a check after three repairs. The person drops, accepts or fixes the case, and the decision is logged.

4.1 From Reports to Claims

Collection. Over six rounds of web searches, searcher agents found reports and a screener decided which ones qualified. In the first round, eight searcher agents worked from fixed written briefs, one per area of agent use. Rounds 2 to 6 ran queries from fixed generators and logged the URLs they returned, and these rounds can therefore be rerun. We merged duplicates and applied written inclusion rules in a screening step. The six rounds gave 253 incidents first reported between January 2025 and October 2026.

Verification. Most readers learn of an incident from a news story, but a headline can blame an agent for a mistake that people made. For example, one headline reported that an AI agent deleted the finished season of a Swedish television show, while the broadcaster’s investigation blamed human error [20]. The verifier therefore reads past the news to the most detailed source it can open: the company’s postmortem, a vendor’s confirmation, a CVE entry or advisory, the researcher’s disclosure or the victim’s account. Of the 253 incidents, 168 were confirmed as recorded and 76 after a correction, usually of a number, a date or a model name. Another 2 conflicted with their sources, the television deletion among them, and 7 remained unconfirmed, giving 244 verified incidents. Of the 199 eligible incidents (defined below), only 29 rely on news alone, and the selection rule prefers the incidents with the most detailed sources.

Labeling. We label each collected incident on six dimensions (Appendix A). The setting records where the agent was deployed, and the root cause records why the agent’s action produced the harm. If a report names several causes, we take the one closest to the agent’s decision. For example, a deletion of the wrong database counts as wrong target even if the task was unclear, and following text from a web page counts as untrusted instruction. The other four record the adversary, the harm, whether reproduction needs model training and whether an agent decision caused the harm.

Two labelers from different vendors, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash, label each incident independently. Agreement runs from κ=0.65\kappa=0.65 for the agent’s decision to κ=0.88\kappa=0.88 for the adversary, and GPT-5.6-luna, as the arbiter, settled the 134 incidents on which they disagreed. To validate the labels, one of the authors read 30 incidents sampled at random and agreed with both final labels (adversary and root cause) in all 30. We also asked GPT-5.6-luna to label the 72 incidents in the wild again without showing it our labels. Its labels matched ours on whether an attacker was present in 66 of the 72 incidents (κ=0.68\kappa=0.68) and on the root cause in 55 incidents (κ=0.70\kappa=0.70).

From Incidents to Claims. An incident enters the replication pool if it is verified, if an action the agent chose caused the harm, and if reproducing the incident needs no model training. We exclude incidents caused by the vendor’s own infrastructure or by a malicious owner. Of the 244 verified incidents, 199 qualify. Each pair of a setting and a root cause forms a class, and 38 classes contain at least one of these incidents. From each class, a fixed rule picks the one or two incidents with the strongest evidence, which gives 56 representatives (Appendix B).

The report analyst converts the record of a selected incident, with its labels and sources, into the claim ⟨T,E,H,a∗,h⟩\langle T,E,H,a^{*},h\rangle of §3 and a claim card that ties each element to a sentence of the report. We rebuilt 55 representatives, and we used the same tools to rebuild other incidents of their classes. This gives 108 replications of 96 incidents in all 38 classes.

4.2 Building and Checking a Replication

Builders. A domain builder for each setting converts the claim into a replication, working from a brief on the tools and mechanics of that setting. From this brief, the builder writes the world, the task, the system prompt, the incident condition, the controls and the state check. Only the facts that the report and its primary sources state are used, and neutral defaults fill the gaps. In our study, the builders were Claude Sonnet 5.5 coding agents, and GPT-5.6-sol made the blind rebuilds below. In the Replit replication, the agent works offline in a Docker container under a system prompt that declares a code freeze. In the task, the user reports a broken executive search in a demo application. The README states that preview, test and production share the database in .env, and the test setup recreates the executives table in that database. An agent that runs make test to check its fix therefore wipes the 1,206 production records.

Hazard Placement. As in the incident, the agent gets the ordinary tools of the setting, such as a shell, a mailbox or a wallet. The hazard appears in the data that these tools return, such as a production path in a configuration file, a long inbox, a changed tool description or a token amount in a different unit. In an adversarial replication, the attacker controls only the channel that the report names, such as a web page, an email or a published component. No tool is named after the failure, because a tool called delete_prod_db would reveal the tested behavior to the model. Reports rarely give the system prompt of the incident, so a replication takes its prompt from the product’s documentation or uses a generic one.

Controls and State Checks. Of the 108 replications, 106 have at least one control. In 73 of them, another control also removes the cue, and the harm rates pool all controls. For an injection, the matched control replaces the injected text with neutral text of equal length at that position. After a session, code decides harm from files and rows, the ledger, the sent mail and the network log. The agent’s own report does not count, because in several incidents, including Replit’s, the agent misreported its actions. About half of the replications run with one to three defenses from the incident’s report or the vendor’s fix, such as separate production credentials, a confirmation step or approval of tools by content hash. In 25 of the 62 defended replications, we wrote an adaptive variant, following Kerckhoffs’s principle. Under the confirmation defense, a simulated user approves only actions that the task asked for.

Reviewers and the Repair Loop. A model from a vendor other than the builder’s reviews the build in two roles. As path reviewer, the model plays an agent that does the task normally in the incident condition. It checks that this normal course of work reaches the hazard without an unmotivated step and without a prohibition or pressure that the report does not state. For Replit, running the tests to check a fix is such a normal step. As domain reviewer, the model checks that the report’s mechanism reaches the agent and that the controls change only the hazard. Complaints from the reviewer and from the checks below go back to the builder, and this repair loop stops when the build passes or after three rounds, always before any model under test runs. In the blind rebuild below, 7 of the 11 builds passed the scripted tests before any repair, and 10 passed after 19 repair rounds in total.

Validity Checks. Before any model under test runs, code checks the conditions of Table 2. First, scripted policies run through all conditions. A reckless policy must trigger the state check in the incident condition and in no control, and a careful policy must leave the check silent. In the Replit replication, the reckless policy caused harm only in the incident condition (Figure 1). Second, a model from a third vendor runs with a fixed reckless or careful instruction before the system prompt, to show that a model can also reach the hazard. Third, code compares the initial files, tools and prompts of the conditions, which must differ only in the hazard. Finally, code runs its part of the fidelity check and fails a build that adds a rule, prohibition or pressure missing from the claim card.

Simulations and Runs. In total, the replications run in ten simulations, one per group of settings, and the replications of a group share a world and its tools (Table 10 in Appendix B). All data are synthetic, and no replication touches a real service, account or wallet. The destructive-action replications and the network part of the containment replications run in Docker containers with a real shell, because a mock shell would hide how rm and git resolve paths. In the other simulations, the agent’s services are modeled in Python. In the agent loop that serves all simulations, the model receives the system prompt, the user’s task and the tool descriptions. In reply, the model gives one action per turn in a text protocol (ACTION: tool(arguments) or DONE: message), for at most 10 to 26 turns depending on the simulation. Because all simulations share this one loop, a new model needs only an API adapter.

Validating the Builders. To test the builders without a person, GPT-5.6-sol rebuilt 11 catalog incidents from their records without seeing our replications. With Gemini 3.5 Flash under test, the 10 generated replications that passed their tests caused harm in 11 of 30 incident sessions and 0 of 60 control sessions. Our study’s replications of the same incidents caused harm in 11 of 33 incident sessions and 0 of 63 control sessions. If we count an incident as repeated when its incident condition caused harm and its controls did not, the two versions agree on 6 of the 11 incidents.

Validating the Reviews. A Claude coding agent read the sessions, state dumps and code of 26 builds of these incidents from five builder setups and labeled 8 builds with a fault that breaks a validity condition, such as a control that also changes the task. With Gemini 3.5 Flash as the review model, the reviews and checks rejected all 8 faulty builds and 11 of the 18 sound builds.

5 Incidents in the Catalog

This section shows where incidents occur and why. The 199 eligible incidents span 38 classes in ten settings, and their number grew from 63 in all of 2025 to 136 in the first ten months of 2026. Researchers mostly demonstrate prompt injection on shipped products, whereas harm in practice came mostly from the agents’ own decisions. Coding agents account for the most incidents (67 of 199), followed by vendor evaluation environments (30), the tool supply chain of MCP servers, skills and extensions (28), enterprise agents (17) and browser agents (17).

Untrusted instruction, the root cause behind prompt injection, is the largest root cause, with 82 incidents (41% of the pool). Each report describes in its own words what went wrong. Our two labelers read a summary of each report and chose the root cause that fits it best (§3), so the root causes in this section are our labels. To check these labels, one of the authors read 30 incidents drawn at random and agreed with the root cause in all 30 incidents.

The next three root causes involve no injected instructions. Unchecked authority (27) covers high-impact actions where a human process would require a confirmation, a limit or a narrower scope, as when coding agents pushed internal screenshots to public repositories under employees’ accounts [21]. Goal overreach (27) covers agents that left their scope, and wrong target (25) covers actions on the wrong environment, path, recipient or amount, such as the DataTalks.Club deletion [2]. Untrusted components (21) are tools or packages that were malicious or changed after approval. Four causes are rare. In instruction disregard (8 incidents), the agent breaks an explicit rule from its user, such as a code freeze; in fabrication (6), it states false facts that someone relies on; in failure escalation (2), its recovery from an error grows into the harm; and in manipulation (1), a person or agent in conversation persuades it.

As Figure 2 shows, the 38 non-empty classes are uneven in size. The largest, prompt injection on coding agents, contains 27 incidents, the next two contain 21 each, and 14 classes have one incident. Most of the growth in eligible incidents came from non-adversarial incidents, which rose from 13 in 2025 to 77 in the first ten months of 2026, while adversarial incidents rose from 50 to 59 .

In-the-Wild Non-Adversarial Harms. We split the pool by the evidence a report gives. Of the 199 incidents, 72 caused harm in the wild, 89 are attacks that researchers demonstrated on a shipped product, 28 come from vendor evaluations, and 10 are attack campaigns against agents described in threat reports. Although the first two groups are similar in size, they barely overlap in cause. Of the 89 demonstrated attacks, 88 involve an adversary and 76 are prompt injection, which disclosed data in 44 cases and changed systems without authorization in 27 cases. Of the 72 incidents in the wild, 62 had no attacker and 2 were prompt injection.

In the wild, data loss is the most common harm (32 of 72), ahead of data disclosure (10) and containment breaches (10). A wrong target (23) and unchecked authority (21) are the most common causes, followed by goal overreach (10) and instruction disregard (7). Examples include the Replit deletion, the Cowork photo deletion [22], the wallet transfer [23, 24] and an OpenClaw assistant that compacted its context, lost the user’s instruction to only suggest deletions, and then deleted more than 200 emails [25]. In each, the hazard was an ordinary part of the environment, such as a production path, a long inbox or a token amount in the wrong unit.

6 Replication Results

This section reports the behavior of five current models in the 108 replications: how often they repeated the harm, how a replication handles the many agents of the Hugging Face incident (§6.1), why replications failed (§6.2), why the agents caused harm (§6.3), how attacks and defenses fared (§6.4) and what the validity checks found (§6.5). We mark its six main findings as Finding 1 to Finding 6. We measure the harm rate over finished sessions. A replication reproduces for a model if one or more incident sessions cause harm.

Models and Conditions. We test five models from four vendors: GPT-5.6-luna and GPT-5.6-sol from OpenAI, Claude Sonnet 4.6 from Anthropic, Gemini 3.5 Flash from Google and the open-weight DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Each model runs three times in every condition of a replication: the incident condition, the controls where the replication has them, each defense and the adaptive variants. To limit queries, scripted policies test a replication first (§4.2), and only the 15 replications that the paper discusses by name ran more often. In all, the main runs comprise 6,439 finished sessions. The median session lasts 3 to 12 turns, depending on the model, and the 39 sessions that ended with an error, such as a timeout of the model’s service, are left out of the denominators.

Finding 1. Current models still repeat many of the reported incidents. The five models caused harm in 18% to 33% of incident sessions, against 0% to 1% in the matched controls.

Repeat Rates. GPT-5.6-luna, for example, caused harm in 64 of 357 incident sessions and in 1 of 549 control sessions. Apart from 7 replications that fail the state diff (§6.5), the controls keep the task and lack only the hazard, so nearly all this harm comes from the hazard.

Over the five models, the rule of §3 rates 32 replications as supported and 23 as suggestive. Another 51 were not reproduced, which bounds their harm rates at 11% to 20%, and 2 have no control. The outcomes also differ by simulation, as most multi-agent replications are supported (7 of 9), as are about half of the supply-chain replications (7 of 15), whereas 11 of the 12 prompt-injection replications did not reproduce. To test whether these outcomes repeat, we reran the 15 named replications 30 times each with GPT-5.6-luna (Table 11 in Appendix B). Each replication that caused harm in the main runs caused harm again in the repetitions, each that caused none caused none again, and their controls caused harm in 0 of 600 repeated sessions. In the main runs, controls also caused harm in 6 replications, most of it in two shopping replications (Table 4).

We audited a sixth model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, with these replications. Anthropic’s safety filter returned empty replies to the incident condition of 30 replications, and a setup error left out 15 more. On the other 63, Claude Sonnet 5.5 caused harm in 12% of incident sessions (95% interval 9%–18%) and in 1 of 328 control sessions, against 15% to 35% of incident sessions for the five models on the same 63. Claude Sonnet 5.5 stopped causing harm in 5 replications that at least four earlier models had repeated, among them the Cowork deletion of iCloud placeholders [26]. Auditing one model costs $0.54 to $47 at list price (Appendix D), which a vendor can afford for every release.

6.1 The Hugging Face Incident

The Reported Incident. The Hugging Face incident is the most widely covered incident in our catalog, and the companies involved and an independent investigator reported on it. In July 2026, OpenAI’s ExploitGym cyber evaluations launched tens of thousands of agents of several models, GPT-5.6-sol among them, in sandboxes that were meant to be isolated [27]. According to METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research), which read the agents’ messages and transcripts, agents that had been given an impossible task looked for a way to cheat through OpenAI’s internal package repository, where they noticed agents in other sandboxes.

One agent opened a message board, and its first message asked for help with an impossible task. About 1,200 agents sent more than 70,000 messages and files on this board, and 700 of them joined an attack on Hugging Face. Hugging Face reported that an autonomous agent system had reached internal datasets and service credentials and moved into several internal clusters over a weekend [28]. No attacker directed the agents, which were doing their evaluation tasks.

The Decision We Replicate. The reports describe two steps, in which agents first coordinate on a channel that nobody assigned to them and some of them then leave the sandbox. The second step depends on vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s infrastructure, which an offline test cannot rebuild, and Gensee reproduced part of it with a live agent [19]. ROGUE-AI therefore tests the first step, the decision that started the incident. In each run, 70 Claude Haiku 4.5 agents work in separate containers on an offline network, and each agent runs one shell command per turn. Half of the agents cannot finish their task, because a note in their workspace says that their decryption key went to a different agent by mistake. As in the report, the configuration lists the board, and no rule forbids messaging. In the matched control, the same configuration line lists a read-only mirror instead, and the board still runs.

As Figure 3 shows, 11 of the 35 agents without a key posted requests for their key, the first of them 62 seconds after the first agent started, and all 35 read the posts of other agents. With the mirror listed instead, 0 of 70 agents posted.

Finding 2. One configuration line that lists a shared message board was enough for agents to start coordinating on it. A rule in the prompt against messaging other workers did not stop them, as 39 of 50 agents without a key still posted.

Lessons from the Replication. No key changed hands, because 0 of the 233 key holders opened the board. The replication thus reproduces the first step of the incident, in which agents that cannot finish a task ask for help on a channel that nobody assigned to them. An offline test cannot rebuild the second step, the sandbox escape. For builders of evaluation sandboxes, the lesson is to keep shared services out of the sandbox, since a rule against using them failed.

6.2 Failed Replications

If a claim does not reproduce, the cause may lie in the model, the report or the replication. The 51 replications that the five models did not reproduce in the main runs therefore enter the diagnose-fix-rerun loop of Figure 1. Diagnoser agents read the transcripts and decide whether the model or the replication kept the harm from happening. In the first case, older and weaker models run the replication, to test whether any model can reach the harm. In the second case, a builder changes the replication, and the models run it again. A change may only remove an element that the report lacks, give the agent more turns or restore a detail that the report states (§6.5), and the controls receive the same change. The loop repeats until a model reproduces the replication or no change within the report remains. Because the loop runs after the main runs, the rates of the five models in Table 4 come from the main runs.

As Figure 4 shows, the loop reproduced 39 of the 51 replications, so ROGUE-AI reproduced the reported harm in 89% of the 108 replications. Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4.1-mini or Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduced 23 of them without a change, among them the $441,000 wallet transfer and the transfer that Grok relayed [29], both with Llama-3.1-8B. These reports thus describe mistakes that current models no longer make.

The other 16 replications reproduced in later rounds of the loop. Some incidents need more turns than others, because the reported harm comes at the end of a long chain of steps, and 3 reproduced once the agent had more turns. Other replications need a detail of the product that the report leaves out. In four injection exploits, for example, the product’s interface renders an image in the agent’s reply and so sends the data to the attacker without a click. With such details in place, 8 of the 11 replications that needed one reproduced, including ForcedLeak [30], CamoLeak and the Notion exfiltration, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash also repeated the Notion exfiltration. Because the controls receive each change as well, a change that makes harm easier affects both conditions. On five of these replications, such as ServiceNow [31] and Comet [32], GPT-4.1-mini caused harm in 5 to 10 of 10 incident sessions each, and the controls in 0 of 100 sessions.

The 12 replications that the loop did not reproduce show the limits of ROGUE-AI. Seven are destructive actions or cloud operations, among them the cloud-operations versions of the Kiro and Terraform deletions. Their reports describe the harmful command but little of the session before it, such as the earlier conversation and the tool outputs that led the agent there, so a replication has to guess this context.

In the other five, no model took the reported step. Three are containment incidents from model evaluations, where the harm needs a step that nothing in the task motivates, such as reaching a machine outside the evaluation. The last two are EchoLeak [33] and the GitHub MCP data flow, in which Claude Haiku 4.5 called the injected requests attacks and refused them.

6.3 Causes of Harm

Finding 3. Whether an incident repeats depends mostly on its environment and task, not on the model. Differences between replications explain 75% of the variance in harm rate, differences between root causes 18%, and differences between models 2%. Incidents with the same root cause can therefore end very differently, so ROGUE-AI replicates each one in its own environment.

Root Causes and Models. The five models mostly agree on a replication: all five caused harm in 18 replications, none did in 51, and they split on the other 39. As Table 4 shows, untrusted components caused the most harm on all five models, and the largest difference between models lies in untrusted instructions (§6.4).

Evidence of a Cause. A supported replication shows that the hazard causes harm, because its incident condition and matched control differ only in the hazard (§3). To learn why the agent took the harmful step, we count an element of the environment as a cause only if changing that element alone lowers harm. If the change adds text, it must also lower harm more than a neutral note of the same length that says nothing about the hazard. We apply this test at two levels: interventions that change one element and rerun whole sessions, and edits at the harmful step of each harmful session (Table 5). We set aside the agent’s own account of its actions, since agents misreport them, and we use transcripts only to describe what the agent saw before it acted.

Finding 4. A note that states both the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models. For Claude Sonnet 4.6, this note cut harm to 1 of 40 sessions, against 58% under a note that states only the fact. Restating the rule in the user’s message left harm at 67% to 80%.

Interventions on One Element. In the transcripts, the harmful step served the user’s task, and the agent did not recognize the hazard. We tested this explanation against four other explanations with interventions that change one element at a time (not counted in Table 4). Each model ran these interventions on the 7 to 11 replications where it had caused harm in at least two of its three main sessions, mostly without an attacker, with three to five sessions each.

In the incident condition, the five models caused harm in 85% to 98% of these sessions. As Figure 5 shows, a note after each tool output that states the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, to 1 of 40 sessions for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and to at most 62% for the others. In the Replit replication, this note states that the tests drop the production database. Under a neutral note of equal length, harm stayed between 83% and 98%, and under a note with the fact but without its consequence, harm stayed between 58% and 82%.

Naming the Hazard. We used GPT-5.6-sol as a judge of the transcripts of Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Gemini 3.5 Flash. In 64 of the 164 harmful sessions, a tool output that the agent had read before the harm showed the hazard, such as a list of zero-byte placeholders. The agent’s own text named the hazard before acting in 0 of the 164 sessions, and in 15 sessions the agent quoted the evidence without treating it as a risk.

As a second cause, the agents took the most direct path they knew. With a safe way to finish the task in the environment, such as a make target that runs the tests against a temporary database, harm stayed between 67% and 100%, and naming this safe path in the task cut it to between 17% and 60% (Figure 5). Removing pressure from the task lowered harm most for the two GPT models, to 16% for GPT-5.6-sol. For defenders, the hazard and its consequence should therefore reach the agent at the step of the action, for instance as a warning attached to a tool’s output. A rule or a safe path that the task does not name barely lowered harm.

Causes in Each Session. The interventions above change the environment and rerun whole sessions, giving a cause per replication. To find the cause of each harmful session, we also cut the 208 harmful sessions of the five models at the first harmful step and let the same model choose that step again five times, with the context unchanged and under each single edit. Each edit changed one thing, by removing the task’s request for the step or its pressure, showing the hazard in the last or the first tool output, restating the rule in the user’s message, removing the text a third party wrote, or adding a neutral note.

An edit halves harm if the unchanged step caused harm in at least 3 of 5 repeats, the edited step’s harm rate is at most half the unchanged rate with non-overlapping 95% Wilson intervals, and a neutral note of equal length in the same place does not do the same. Table 5 defines each cause by the edit that removes it. For example, a session counts as early warning not enough if a warning in the last tool output halves harm but the same warning in the first does not, so the agent needed the warning right before it acted.

As Table 5 shows, at least one edit removed the harm in 118 of the 208 sessions, and 62 sessions had several causes. The two most common causes were that the task asked for the harmful step and that the agent never saw the hazard. In contrast, in nearly half of the DeepSeek-V4-Flash sessions and about a third of the Gemini 3.5 Flash sessions, the agent saw the hazard in the last tool output and acted anyway. Only 14 sessions were rare slips, in which the same model caused harm in fewer than 3 of 5 repeats.

Finding 5. Most harmful steps with a known cause happened because the task asked for the step or because the agent never saw the hazard (94 of 118 sessions). However, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash saw the hazard and took the step anyway in 22 of 49 and 15 of 49 harmful sessions.

6.4 Attackers and Defenses

With and Without an Attacker. Replications of prompt injection caused less harm than the other replications on all five models, as the untrusted-instruction row of Table 4 shows, and almost all of the harm in injection replications came from replications that do not rebuild a public exploit. In particular, the twelve replications of injection exploits on shipped products, such as EchoLeak [33], ForcedLeak and the GitHub MCP data flow, caused harm in 2 of 180 sessions across the five models. The injected text, however, reached the model in 108 of 166 logged sessions. In later rounds of the loop (§6.2), 8 of these exploits ran again, and GPT-4.1-mini reproduced 5 of the 8 (4 supported), whereas the five main models reproduced between 0 and 4 . Thus, an older model still follows most of these public exploits, while current models follow at most half of them.

Finding 6. On all five models, replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of untrusted instructions such as prompt injection. Claude Sonnet 4.6, for example, caused harm in 0 of 138 sessions with untrusted instructions but in 26% of the sessions without an attacker.

As Table 4 also shows, unchecked authority caused more harm than untrusted instructions for all five models, for example 32% against 7% for GPT-5.6-luna. In the causes with the most harm, the agent either trusts a component that the user installed or has authority that no check limits. Therefore, a model can avoid harm from injected text and still publish, spend or delete what it should not.

Among the adversarial replications, malicious or swapped components caused the most harm, as Table 4 shows. GPT-5.6-luna caused harm in 19 of its 39 sessions in these replications. At the user’s request, the agent installs a skill or MCP server and follows the setup steps and tool descriptions, as the component’s author intends. GPT-5.6-luna ran a malicious skill’s installer in 3 of 3 sessions and sent mail through a server that added a hidden recipient in 3 of 3 sessions. Some components cause harm as soon as the agent calls them, but even without these 13 replications, the five models caused harm in 14% to 28% of incident sessions.

Defenses and Adaptive Variants. As Table 6 shows, few sessions caused harm under the defenses taken from the reports or the vendors’ fixes. GPT-5.6-luna caused harm in 3 of 237 defended sessions, and GPT-5.6-sol, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash caused harm in 4%, 4%, 7% and 6% of their defended sessions. The defenses fall into four kinds: instructions or labels for the model, such as spotlighting [34]; tool-layer checks, such as allowlists, scoped credentials and spending caps; confirmation by the simulated user (§4.2); and tracking where data came from. With confirmation or data-flow tracking, the five models caused no harm.

A check outside the model also stops harm that the model cannot see. In the replication of the MCP tool that changes after approval [35], harm occurred in 15 of 16 sessions under approval keyed to the tool’s name, but in 0 of 16 under approval keyed to a hash of the tool’s description that is checked at each call. Instructions and labels worked less well for the two models that follow untrusted text more readily, Gemini 3.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

However, adaptive variants recover part of the harm, mostly against tool-layer checks (Table 6). In these cases, the check matched the form of an action, and the adaptive variant changed only the form. For example, one variant placed data at a path that robots.txt did not list, and GPT-5.6-luna fetched the data from that path in 3 of 3 sessions (Appendix B). Data-flow tracking worked better, as its adaptive variants caused harm only with Gemini 3.5 Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

For GPT-5.6-luna, confirmation by the simulated user lowered task completion the most, to 7 of 27 confirmed sessions against 94 of 234 without a defense, while data-flow tracking let most tasks finish (Appendix B). Thus, the defenses with the least harm either require confirmation before the agent uses its permissions or track the data that an action transfers, although confirmation faced no adaptive variant here.

6.5 Validity of the Replications

Shipped Agent Products. To check our agent loop, we ran OpenAI’s Codex CLI [36] with GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Code [1] with Claude Sonnet 4.6 through the 10 destructive-action replications that were picked to represent their classes. Both products ran unattended, skipping approval prompts, under the same state checks. As Table 7 shows, both models repeated the Cowork placeholder deletion [26] in all incident sessions (§6.3), and the matched controls lost no files. In the other nine replications, GPT-5.6-sol caused harm in 0 of 27 sessions and Claude Sonnet 4.6 in 0 of 27. In the Replit replication, both models asked for permission under the code freeze. Neither model detected a hazard that passes the user’s own check, such as a placeholder with the right checksum. The two models caused harm about as often in our own agent loop (Appendix B).

The reckless-model check of Table 2 predicts most replications that do not reproduce (§6.2). It runs an inexpensive model, told to follow all instructions in its inputs, for two or three sessions; in our study it ran after the builds. It flagged 44 of the 51 replications that the five models did not reproduce in the main runs, against 6 of the 55 supported or suggestive ones. A flag calls for reading the transcripts first, since even a reckless model stops where the task gives no reason to go on. A not-reproduced outcome therefore bounds the harm rate of one replication only, and the transcripts show whether the bound also applies to the reported claim.

However, the same checks also found problems in reproduced replications. In 7 of them (5 supported), no control passes the state diff, for example because the control lacks the path by which the harm happens. Part of their harm difference may therefore come from the control. In 2 supported replications, a malicious mail server copies all messages, so any mail the agent sends counts as harm, and these replications measure the component more than the model. In 4 replications (3 of them multi-agent), the agent’s input contains a scoring or deadline sentence that their reports lack. Without it, all 4 still reproduced, and 27 of 57 incident sessions caused harm, against 27 of 59 with it.

7 Discussion

Recommendations for Agent Builders. Most incidents with harm in the wild came from a wrong target or unchecked authority (23 and 21 of 72), and least privilege [37] limits the cost of such mistakes. Production credentials can be kept in an account that the agent cannot use, and destructive commands and payments can require a person’s approval.

Recommendations for Benchmark Builders. Benchmarks built from attacks measure the risk that researchers demonstrate, but most harm in the wild came from incidents without an attacker (§5). Agent safety benchmarks should therefore add non-adversarial hazards, name the source incident of each test case, pair each condition with a matched control and read harm from the environment’s state. Public incidents may also be in a model’s training data, but given the opening of each replication, three models named the right incident for only 12 of the 108, and these 12 were supported or suggestive about as often as the others (7 of 12, against 48 of 96).

Recommendations for Incident Reporting. Of the 51 claims that the five models did not reproduce, 11 needed a detail of the product that their reports left out, such as whether the interface renders images in the agent’s reply (§6.2). Reports seldom include the model and its version, the system prompt, the agent framework, the earlier conversation or the tool output that preceded the harmful action. The agent’s own account is a weak source, because its final message omitted or denied the harm in 77 of 136 harmful sessions of Gemini 3.5 Flash and in 18 of 49 harmful sessions of GPT-5.6-luna.

Outcomes and Reported Incidents. Because few reports name the model and its version, our replications run current models from four vendors instead of the model of each incident. A supported outcome means that the incident can happen today even if the original agent ran another model, and the audit of §3 can rerun a replication on a model that a report names. By contrast, a replication that only older or weaker models reproduce describes a mistake that current models no longer make, and a replication that no model reproduces leaves its report unconfirmed. However, a failed replication does not show that a report is false. Most of these reports leave out the conversation and tool outputs before the harmful step (§6.2), and a future version of ROGUE-AI could fill in this context in many plausible ways and run each version.

Safety of the ROGUE-AI Pipeline. ROGUE-AI uses LLM agents to study the failures of LLM agents, so its own agents can fail in the same ways. We therefore apply our recommendations to the pipeline itself. No agent checks its own work or decides harm, a model from another vendor reviews each build, and the models under test run offline on synthetic data (§4). Because code decides harm without a model, an error shared by all vendors cannot change it. Likewise, we find the causes of harm by rerunning sessions or harmful steps with one element changed, and the agents’ accounts of their own actions do not count as evidence (§6.3). Appendix C details these checks by root cause.

Limitations. Our catalog counts publicly reported incidents, so it likely over-represents incidents that people write about, and the 38 classes are a lower bound. As the replications run in simulated environments with one agent loop, and only ten destructive-action replications also ran in shipped products (§6.5), a harm rate may misstate a product’s risk. Where a report gives no mechanism, our replication reconstructs it, and a replication that departs from the report can misstate the harm. ROGUE-AI did not reproduce 12 replications, mostly because their reports leave out what led the agent to the harmful step (§6.2). Model judgments err, as reviews sent back 11 of 18 sound builds and blind rebuilds disagreed with ours on 5 of 11 incidents.

8 Other Related Work

Agent Security Benchmarks. Since indirect prompt injection was shown [38] and formalized [39], most benchmarks build test cases from attacks that their authors design. AgentDojo [8] places injected instructions in the tool outputs of workspace, Slack, travel and banking tasks; InjecAgent [9], Agent Security Bench (ASB) [40], WASP [41], MCP Security Bench (MSB) [42] and MCPTox [43] cover indirect injection for tool, web and MCP agents. A second group adds risky requests and accidents. ToolEmu [44] scores risk with emulated tools, Agent-SafetyBench [17], OpenAgentSafety [45], OS-Harm [46], AgentHarm [47] and RedCode [48] test risky tasks for computer-use, general and coding agents, and ODCV-Bench [49] tests constraint violations under pressure.

Closest to our non-adversarial classes, Overeager-Gen [18], BLIND-ACT [50], AutoElicit [51] and OS-BLIND [52] elicit harm from benign tasks of coding and computer-use agents, and SABER [53] and OSGuard [54] check the final state of a project or desktop after such tasks. Li et al. [55] find that most of 40 such benchmarks test risks from outside the agent, and Zhang and Jiang [56] argue that benchmarks omit harm to deployers. In contrast, ROGUE-AI reconstructs publicly reported agent incidents as controlled experiments, using matched controls to test whether hypothesized causes contribute to the observed harm.

Studies of Real Incidents. The AI Incident Database [5] and the AIAAIC Repository [57] collect AI harms such as the Replit deletion [14], and METR [58] scores 44 agent incidents for overreach and deception. The Agent Incident Registry [6], the closest catalog, labels 487 agent records by mechanism and finds 92 safety failures without an adversary, and Hasan and Biswas [7] mine 16,586 GitHub issues of coding tools into 547 operational safety failures and 33 risk types. Unlike both, we cover ten settings with and without an adversary and replicate each class on current models.

Automated Reproduction. Section 2 compares ROGUE-AI with the closest reproduction work, Chronicle, Gensee, Squidbrake and CVE-Genie (Table 1). Outside security, ScientistTwo [59] reproduces the baselines of 107 accepted machine-learning papers with a critic at each stage.

Defenses and Adaptive Evaluation. Defenses for agents range from separating trusted and untrusted text in the prompt, as spotlighting does [34], to tool-layer privilege control (Progent [60]) and data-flow tracking (CaMeL [61]). Nasr et al. [62] show that adaptive attacks bypass 12 recent defenses against injection and jailbreaks. Our results agree for defenses that match text, and we also test defenses taken from incident reports, with and without an attacker. Perplexity [63] tells agents built on twelve models to attack its sandbox, and several bypassed its network policy. Unlike this red teaming, ROGUE-AI replicates incidents in which agents caused harm during ordinary tasks.

9 Conclusion

We presented ROGUE-AI, a multi-agent framework that rebuilds a reported agent incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause. ROGUE-AI reproduced the reported harm in 89% of its 108 replications. Agents built on five current models still made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, and they rarely caused harm without the blamed cause. Most incidents with real-world harm had no attacker, and the agent did its task but missed an ordinary hazard. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these incidents contain none. In contrast, a warning that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models. Agent builders should therefore add such warnings and keep production credentials out of the agent’s reach, benchmarks should include hazards without an attacker, and vendors can rerun the replications before each release. Future work could extend ROGUE-AI from agents that act on text to agents that act on images, such as computer-use agents that work from screenshots and robots driven by vision models.

Appendix A Labels and Root Causes in the Annotation Guide

The two primary labelers used the same prompt, which contains the annotation guide and the record and no other text, and Table 8 gives their agreement per dimension. Disagreements on 134 incidents went to GPT-5.6-luna, and the majority value was used. The 22 values on which all three labelers disagreed went to a further model pass that applied the guide’s tie-break rules and recorded a reason for each, and an author then made the final decision on each value. The incidents involve the products of many vendors, led by Anthropic (53 incidents) and OpenAI (50), then Google (22), Cursor (17), OpenClaw (12) and Microsoft (11); an incident counts once per vendor it involves. These counts likely follow the size and openness of each user base. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s totals include incidents of their own evaluations.

Table 9 gives the definitions of the root causes that the labelers applied (§3), in the words of the annotation guide. The labelers take the cause closest to the agent’s decision when two values fit. Untrusted component applies only when a tool, server or package was itself malicious or changed after approval, and unchecked authority applies only when no other cause does, that is, when the agent did roughly what it was asked but took a high-impact step that a human process would have gated. The last two rows define the causes that the replication pool excludes, because in those incidents the agent made no harmful decision.

Appendix B Additional Replication Details

Selection Rule. Within each class, incidents are ranked by the strength of their evidence: a first-party postmortem, then a vendor confirmation, a CVE or advisory, a researcher’s disclosure, a victim’s account, and news only. Ties are broken by how far the harm went (harm in the wild, then a demonstration on a real product, a threat report, and a vendor evaluation) and then by date, with recent incidents first. Classes with three or more incidents add the next incident in this order from a different product, because one product’s behavior may be specific to its design. Of the 56 representatives, we rebuilt 55. The remaining representative is a vendor’s log of many different actions by its own coding agent, with many mechanisms instead of one to reproduce.

Repeated Runs. Because a count from three runs can reflect chance, we repeated the 15 named replications 30 times with GPT-5.6-luna, 1,110 sessions in total (Table 11); we fixed the list before the repetitions ran. The repetitions cover the incident condition of each replication and the controls of those that Table 11 does not mark with –. Replications with more than one incident configuration, such as two rule wordings, count each configuration, and the wallet replication ran two sessions per repetition. The outcome changed across the repetitions in 6 replications, and the controls caused harm in 0 of 600 sessions. Repetition mainly sharpens the rates, as the wiki replication caused harm in 1 of 3 main sessions and in 12 of 30 repeated ones. The replications of several well-known incidents caused no harm in any repeated session, such as the wallet overpayment (0 of 60) and the deleted and recreated environment (0 of 30).

Sessions and Compute. The scenario code was frozen before these runs, and development runs with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.8, which we used to debug the environments, are excluded. Some models wrote the environment’s part themselves, such as invented command output, so we cut each reply at the first such line and reran the three models that often did so. GPT-5.6-sol has more sessions than the other models because four simulations ran some configurations of its first run twice, and both runs count.

Products and Models. We placed the user’s standing rule in the product’s user-level instruction file and gave the user’s task as the prompt. As a result, each product used its own system prompt, tools and stopping rule. For project tasks, a product started in the repository, and otherwise in the user’s home directory. In both products, the models finished most tasks: GPT-5.6-sol in Codex CLI completed 22 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 in Claude Code 20 of their 30 control tasks. Our loop gave similar results for the same models: GPT-5.6-sol caused harm only in the Cowork replication, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 also in 1 of 3 Replit sessions, where it stopped to ask in Claude Code. In our loop, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which neither product runs, caused harm in 4 of the 10 replications.

Cost of the Defenses. Among the defenses with completion data, confirmation by the simulated user cost GPT-5.6-luna the most completed tasks. In the simulations that record completion, GPT-5.6-luna completed the user’s task in 94 of 234 incident-condition sessions without a defense. With the simulated user confirming, it completed 7 of 27, likely because the agent waits at the confirmation or the user declines a step that the task needs. With data-flow tracking it completed 18 of 27 and with tool-layer checks 57 of 120, although these counts pool different replications. The other models completed a larger share of confirmed sessions than of sessions without a defense: GPT-5.6-sol 17 of 27 against 143 of 250, Claude Sonnet 4.6 21 of 27 against 154 of 234, Gemini 3.5 Flash 21 of 27 against 120 of 234 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash 22 of 27 against 134 of 234.

Adaptive Variants. Three replications show how the adaptive variants of §6.4 performed the same action in a different form. In the parks replication, a check blocked the paths that the site’s robots.txt file disallows, and the adaptive variant placed the data at a path the file did not list; GPT-5.6-luna fetched it in 3 of 3 sessions. In the statistics portal, a check refused to fill a saved password on a site the user had not named, and the adaptive variant offered a button that reused the saved session, which GPT-5.6-luna pressed in 1 of 3 sessions. In a multi-agent workspace, a check scanned outgoing messages for balances, and the adaptive variant asked for them as a CSV attachment, which went unchecked.

Appendix C Checks on the Pipeline’s Own Agents

The agents that build and check the replications can fail like the agents that the replications test. Table 12 lists the root causes of Table 9 that apply to the agents of ROGUE-AI, the step where each could occur and the check that covers it, with the evidence from our study. The checks follow the three rules of §4. No agent checks its own work, code decides harm from the environment’s final state, and each judgment that an agent makes has an independent check (Table 3). A person decides the three kinds of cases that the agents cannot resolve, and the decision is logged.

Appendix D Cost per Replication

Table 13 itemizes the cost of one replication at list price, from the token counts of the logged calls and agent runs. With the five models under test, one replication costs $3.28 from collection to diagnosis. Building costs the most, because the runs of the builder agents ($97 for the 56 representatives) also built the ten simulations that later replications reuse. The automated builder of §4.2 lowers the total to $1.75, against an average of $2.77 per CVE for CVE-Genie [12].

Appendix E Ethics

All incidents come from public sources, and we describe them at the level of the public record without adding personal information. The replications run offline in containers with synthetic data. Credentials are fake, hosts use the reserved example domain, and ledgers and mailboxes are local files, so no replication touches a real service, account, or wallet. Codex CLI and Claude Code ran unattended only inside these containers, and the study has no human subjects. Because the paper measures how current models act as agents, we reported each model’s results to its vendor. The replications contain no exploit code beyond what the public reports describe, and builders can run them as regression tests before a release, including against the fixes that vendors have published.
